title: Your idea sucks, now go do it anyway: the first idea rarely survives, so start and iterate
summary: Jason Cohen argues that a founder's first idea is probably wrong and rarely matters, because the real business emerges from building and watching what happens. He cites PayPal, Flickr and his own Smart Bear as companies that pivoted away from weak initial ideas. Waiting for a perfect idea is the mistake; a small market is enough to start.

principles.text: Your first idea probably sucks, and it doesn't matter, because the business will likely turn into something different.
principles.quote: Your idea probably sucks, and it doesn't matter because your business will probably turn out to be something completely different.

principles.text: Don't wait for a fully fleshed-out idea before starting; the right idea only appears by trying the wrong one.
principles.quote: the only way to find the right one is to try the wrong one and see what happens. You won't find it by fiddling around with PowerPoint slides and Photoshop mock-ups.

principles.text: Follow what users actually value in the product; Flickr emerged because testers cared about sharing more than real-time chat.
principles.quote: people were interested in the *sharing* part more than the *real-time* part.

principles.text: Expect to cut most of your product lineup; of six tools Smart Bear sold, only one mattered in the end.
principles.quote: At one point we were selling six different tools; the only one that mattered in the end was Code Reviewer.

principles.text: A tiny market is enough to bootstrap; you'll figure out the rest once you've started (Cohen quotes Neil Davidson).
principles.quote: A $50,000 market opportunity is enough to get you off the ground--once you get started you'll figure out the rest.
